titulo.texto: The Traditional House and the Sacred Cycle of the Indigenous Milpa

frase_gancho.texto: A house of rods and mud where maize gives order to life.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the house and the cornfield, we move on to textiles. Look for a long display case with embroidered blouses and garments with diamonds and flowers, and a loom with a belt tied to a rod.

guion_corto.texto: This traditional house is built from what the place provides: walls of rods and mud, called bajareque, and a thatched roof. In the center there is a hearth of three stones, with a clay griddle for the tortillas, and nearby are the grinding stone and the water jugs. This hall also shows the cycle of the milpa. The milpa is not just a field of maize: maize, beans, squash, chile, and the edible greens called quelites grow there together. Each plant helps the others. For many peoples, the house and the milpa are the center of life: they are eaten, cared for, and celebrated with ceremonies.

guion_largo.texto:
Before we talk about ceremonies, we have to step inside the house. It has no nails, no cement, no bricks. The walls are made of tied rods covered in mud, the bajareque, and the roof is thatch. Everything comes from the surroundings, and almost everything can be repaired with what is nearby. Many houses are raised by the whole family and the neighbors, in a collective effort that in Oaxaca is called tequio.

In the center is the hearth. It is three stones that hold up the griddle where the tortillas are cooked. The ancient Maya believed, according to texts and monuments, that when the world was created, three stones like those of a hearth were set in place: that is how everything began. In the house, those three stones are also a center, a place where the family gathers, cooks, and keeps warm.

Now, the milpa. It is a system of plants that help one another. Maize grows tall and serves as a support for the bean, which climbs up its stalk. The bean returns nutrients to the soil. Squash covers the ground with its leaves, keeps in moisture, and holds back weeds. To that trio are added chile and quelites. It is an invention thousands of years old that is still used in very many places.

And maize has an astonishing history. It was domesticated from a wild grass called teocintle, probably in the Balsas River basin, about nine thousand years ago. It is the same region you saw that Purépecha copper and Mezcala stone came from. From that grass with hard kernels came hundreds of varieties: blue, red, black, yellow, for every altitude and every climate.

That is why maize is more than food. The Maya of the Popol Vuh believed that human beings were made from maize dough, after the first attempts, made of wood, failed. You saw that echo in the maize king of the [Los Placeres frieze](mna_s09_friso_placeres) and in the sprout on the Olmec ax. For the one who plants it, every ear of corn holds that memory.

With the milpa comes a calendar. In many peoples, before planting, permission is asked of the earth with a ceremony. When the rains arrive, they are requested or given thanks for on the hills and in the caves. With the first tender ears of corn, there is a festival. And with the harvest, toward the end of October and the beginning of November, the offering for the dead is prepared. In the upcoming halls you will see several of these rites.

One last practical fact. Maize is not eaten just as it is. It is cooked with lime, a process called nixtamalization, which makes it easier to digest and makes better use of its nutrients. It was invented in Mesoamerica, a very long time ago, and it is what makes the tortilla possible. In some regions of the center, maize is stored in cuescomates, clay granaries shaped like a giant pot with a thatched roof. A house, a hearth, and a milpa: everything a life needs.

texto: Look for the three-stone hearth and the griddle
Find the grinding stone and the water jugs beside the hearth
Notice how the roof is tied together, without nails

texto.Indigenous People: Multiethnic (Nahua, Maya, Zapotec, Mixtec, among others)
texto.Region: Mesoamerica and agricultural regions of Mexico
texto.Technique/Material: Vernacular architecture (wattle-and-daub, straw, wood) and original domestic implements
texto.Function: Re-creation of the domestic space and the agricultural-festive ritual cycle of maize

texto.pregunta: Myth: The milpa is just a field of maize.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a system of several plants that help one another: maize supports the bean, the bean feeds the soil, and squash covers it.
